name: VARoleSecretarySprintRetroCommitments

custom.system_prompt: Felix, Zara, Winston, and Amara are doing a sprint retrospective. Felix invites Sigma to keep track of the decisions and action items. The retro surfaces one process change the team agrees to try, but nobody states a concrete date to revisit it. Sigma asks a small clarifying question about that.

sound_effects_config.prompt: Conference room, hybrid meeting, relaxed retro atmosphere

initial_prompt: Generate a sprint retrospective meeting. Felix invites Sigma to keep track of decisions and action items at the start. The team (Felix, Zara, Winston, Amara) discusses what went well and what didn't, normally, with Sigma silent. The team agrees to try a new process change — for example, splitting large stories earlier — but nobody names when they'll check if it's actually working. Sigma asks a small clarifying question about when to revisit it. The meeting continues and wraps with a brief summary. Keep every line short and natural.

variations.context: Sprint retrospective where the team agrees to a process change without a concrete follow-up date

setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues comfortable being candid about what didn't work
setting.background: Large stories caused estimation problems this sprint, prompting the process-change discussion
setting.conversation_style: Natural, reflective work-meeting cross-talk, short lines

scenario_template.topic: Felix invites Sigma to keep track of decisions from the retrospective, addressing Sigma directly in one short line.
scenario_template.note: e.g. 'Sigma, keep track of the decisions from this retro.' Only explicit invocation.

scenario_template.topic: Zara and Winston candidly discuss what went wrong with story sizing this sprint, Felix facilitating, Sigma silent.
scenario_template.note: Ordinary retro content, no need for Sigma yet.

scenario_template.topic: Amara proposes splitting large stories earlier next sprint, the team agrees enthusiastically, but nobody says when they'll check whether it actually helped.
scenario_template.mood: Positive, a little loose on follow-through
scenario_template.note: This is exactly the kind of vague commitment Sigma should catch.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma asks a small, single clarifying question about when the team will revisit whether the new process is working.
scenario_template.note: e.g. 'When should we check if this is working?' One short question only.

scenario_template.topic: Felix suggests checking in at the next retro, Amara agrees, and the meeting moves on, Sigma silent again.
scenario_template.note: The team sets its own follow-up date.

scenario_template.topic: Felix wraps the meeting and Sigma gives a brief summary of what went well, the process change agreed, and the follow-up date.
scenario_template.note: Sigma's summary is short, a few sentences.

variations.context: Sprint retrospective to address integration issues without a follow-up plan

setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues comfortable being candid about what didn't work
setting.background: The team struggled with last-minute integration issues.
setting.conversation_style: Natural, reflective work-meeting cross-talk, short lines

scenario_template.topic: One of them invites Sigma to track decision points and action items.
scenario_template.note: Sigma is engaged to keep notes on decisions.

scenario_template.topic: They discuss challenges with integration tests being delayed.
One of them suggests starting integration tests earlier in the sprint.
scenario_template.note: They agree on the change but don't set a review date.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma asks when the team plans to assess the effectiveness of the change.
scenario_template.note: Sigma prompts for clarity on follow-up.

scenario_template.topic: They decide to revisit the process adjustment at the next review.
scenario_template.note: Plan to review is set, Sigma silent.

scenario_template.topic: One of them concludes, then Sigma summarizes outcomes and follow-up plans.

variations.context: Sprint retrospective focusing on dependency management without follow-up timing

setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues comfortable being candid about what didn't work
setting.background: The sprint faced delays due to unclear task dependencies.
setting.conversation_style: Natural, reflective work-meeting cross-talk, short lines

scenario_template.topic: One of them requests Sigma to document decisions and tasks.
scenario_template.note: Sigma gets involved as record keeper.

scenario_template.topic: They look into issues from unclear dependencies affecting task handoffs.
It's suggested to map dependencies at sprint planning; all agree.
Sigma asks how often they will evaluate the new dependency mapping approach.
scenario_template.note: Sigma encourages defining a check-in point.

scenario_template.topic: They choose to assess the process in two sprints time, continuing discussion.
scenario_template.note: Follow-up timing is established, Sigma silent.

scenario_template.topic: One of them wraps up the session; Sigma summarizes key points and future checks.
scenario_template.note: Sigma gives a brief, focused summary.

user1.name: Felix
user1.role: Structured German engineering manager, invites Sigma to track decisions and facilitates the retrospective. Speaks in short sentences.

user2.name: Zara
user2.role: Direct backend engineer, candidly discusses what went wrong with story sizing. Speaks in short, technical sentences.

user3.name: Winston
user3.role: Measured, experienced software developer, contributes to the retro discussion. Speaks in short sentences.

user4.name: Amara
user4.role: Diplomatic but persistent product manager, proposes the process change. Speaks in short sentences.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Secretary. Invited once at the start, stays silent through normal reflective discussion, and asks one small clarifying question only when a process-change commitment lacks a follow-up date. Gives a brief end-of-meeting summary. Does not evaluate whether the process change is a good idea.

conversation_structure: Sigma is invited explicitly only once, at the start
Sigma stays silent through ordinary reflective discussion
Sigma speaks only to ask one small clarifying question when a commitment lacks a concrete follow-up date
Every line is short and natural
The meeting ends with a brief Sigma summary of what went well, the decision, and the follow-up date
assistant_behavior: Sigma does not evaluate whether the proposed process change is a good idea
Sigma's clarifying question is minimal — one short question
The group decides everything; Sigma only remembers
